primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy can generate an IgA-dominant autoimmune response against transglutaminases. In dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermal transglutaminase 3 (TG3) is the dominant cutaneous autoantigen; IgA-TG3 immune deposits accumulate in the papillary dermis, recruit neutrophils, and produce intensely pruritic subepidermal vesicles.
vignette: A 31-year-old man has several months of intensely pruritic, grouped papules and small vesicles on the extensor surfaces of both elbows, knees, and buttocks. Many lesions are excoriated. He has no chronic diarrhea or weight loss. Biopsy of an intact lesion shows neutrophils concentrated at the tips of dermal papillae with subepidermal vesicle formation. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits in the papillary dermis.
lead: IgA autoantibodies in this patient’s skin are most characteristically directed against which antigen?
distractor_notes: Tissue transglutaminase/TG2 is the principal autoantigen of celiac enteropathy and circulating anti-TG2 antibodies are common in gluten-sensitive disease, but TG3 is the dominant cutaneous autoantigen in dermatitis herpetiformis.
Desmoglein 3 is a desmosomal cadherin targeted in pemphigus vulgaris, producing intraepidermal acantholysis and intercellular IgG rather than granular papillary IgA.
BP180 is a hemidesmosomal protein targeted in bullous pemphigoid, which produces tense subepidermal bullae with linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane rather than granular IgA at dermal papillae.
Type VII collagen is the anchoring-fibril target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita; it does not produce the classic gluten-associated granular IgA pattern of dermatitis herpetiformis.
key_expl: The intensely pruritic symmetric eruption on extensor surfaces, neutrophils at dermal papillary tips, subepidermal vesicles, and granular IgA in the papillary dermis identify dermatitis herpetiformis. This disorder is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy even when gastrointestinal symptoms are absent. In celiac enteropathy, the dominant autoantigen is tissue transglutaminase (TG2). In dermatitis herpetiformis, epitope spreading produces high-affinity IgA against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3), and IgA-TG3 complexes localize in the papillary dermis and drive neutrophilic inflammation.
objective: Distinguish the dominant autoantigen of dermatitis herpetiformis (epidermal transglutaminase/TG3) from tissue transglutaminase/TG2 in celiac enteropathy and from structural antigens targeted in other autoimmune blistering diseases.
clues: granular IgA deposits in papillary dermis
